description: We are a passionate web development team (Frontend React/Three.js, Backend Node.js, and Full-Stack) building "LunarRelics 3D" for the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge. We are creating an interactive 3D digital museum and storytelling web platform showcasing historic NASA rovers and hardware left on the Moon and Mars. We welcome UI/UX designers, researchers, and storytellers!
summary: Lunar Relics 3D is a bilingual Arabic–English interactive archive of 16 NASA mission relics across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. It turns dispersed mission records into first-person spacecraft stories, navigable 3D scenes, timelines, hardware hotspots, recorded narration, quick quizzes, badges, and a four-mode Explorer Challenge. Eleven missions use NASA-published 3D meshes; the other five use SI-generated models built to NASA’s published specifications and clearly labeled “not from NASA”, with source links kept visible. The site is responsive, shareable by mission link, and designed for students, families, and casual space learners. It addresses the challenge by making discarded hardware understandable as evidence: what it was built to do, where it went, what it measured, and what remains after the mission ends.
details:
What it does

Lunar Relics 3D is a browser-based, bilingual learning experience about equipment that remained after missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. The archive contains 16 structured records. Each record connects a relic to its mission dates, destination, status, source links, first-person English and Arabic story, timeline, hardware explanations, questions, quiz, badge, and recorded narration. The voice is a storytelling device: the spacecraft speaks in first person, while the interface makes clear which facts and sources support the story.

Visitors begin at a 3D globe-style map with mission pins and can filter the archive by world or 3D availability. Selecting a mission opens a chaptered story beside its 3D scene. Hardware hotspots identify parts and draw the learner toward an explanation of what each part did. The mission timeline then connects hardware to journey and scientific purpose. A quick quiz awards one locally saved badge per mission. The Explorer Challenge adds four playable modes: evidence quiz, mission timeline ordering, launch-era ordering, and “name the machine” model identification.

Guided, accessible exploration

Audio is optional. Every mission has English and Arabic recorded narration for the main story, an introduction, and the hardware points represented in the narration manifest. “Full journey” starts with the introduction, moves through the story and hardware chapters, follows the page while the voice plays, reaches the timeline, and ends at the quiz. Learners can stop, scroll manually, choose a language, or use the text-only path. Mission links encode the mission, world, and language, so a learner can bookmark or share a specific story.

Accuracy and provenance

The project is intentionally honest about representation. Eleven missions use unmodified NASA-published GLB meshes from NASA 3D Resources and are labeled as NASA models. The five missions that have no public NASA mesh (Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Apollo 12 ALSEP, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, Phoenix) use 3D models generated with Super Intelligence from written descriptions of NASA’s published specifications and photographs; every one of them carries the on-screen label “SI-generated model built to published specs · not from NASA”, and the repository’s asset-source file lists them separately. The Spirit entry uses the NASA Opportunity mesh as a representative model of the identical rover design; Pioneer 10 is used as the available model for a record that discusses Pioneer 10 and 11. These limitations are shown rather than hidden. The Moon and Mars globe textures are stored locally, and the Mars height treatment is explicitly visual rather than a scientific elevation model.

Technology and intended impact

The front end uses React 18 and Vite. Three.js, @react-three/fiber, and drei provide the 3D scenes; Tailwind/PostCSS support styling; lucide-react supplies interface icons; canvas-confetti supplies reduced-motion-aware feedback. The Web Audio API handles the optional soundscape and narration routing. GitHub hosts the public source and Vercel hosts the live site. FFmpeg supports audio/video preparation, while Python and Playwright were used for testing and screenshot capture. The repository includes a production build and Node tests for selected experience and asset-integrity behaviors, without claiming exhaustive device certification.

Creatively, the project treats discarded equipment as a collection of voices and evidence rather than a static list of names. It is built for school-age learners, families, teachers, and casual space enthusiasts, especially users who prefer Arabic or need a low-friction phone experience. The team considered RTL layout, bilingual labels and subtitles, keyboard and skip-to-content access, reduced-motion behavior, responsive breakpoints, lazy model loading, capped device pixel ratio, local textures, and a local JSON fallback when an optional API is unavailable. The intended impact is a durable, source-linked path from “what was left behind?” to “what did this machine enable us to learn?”
